claims.text: The transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition is driven by the evolution of local chemical order and phase-boundary morphology.
B2 coarsening produces a percolating coherent network that maximizes anti-phase-boundary density.
At intermediate aging temperatures, local chemical orders nucleate and grow within the FCC phase.
High anti-phase-boundary energy forces dislocations in ordered domains to move as paired superdislocations.
Paired superdislocation motion causes severe order hardening.
Order hardening from the coherent ordered network causes the dramatic loss of ductility.
At higher temperatures, thermally activated cross-slip of superdislocations facilitates dislocation bypass and restores ductility.
Loss of phase-boundary coherency at higher temperatures permits easier dislocation transmission and restores ductility.
Formation of anti-phase boundaries at higher temperatures can facilitate dislocation bypass.
The initial alloy has alternating lamellar FCC and ordered B2 phases with minimal long-range chemical order in the FCC matrix.
Aging at 600–800°C followed by room-temperature tensile testing should access the embrittled state, while aging above 900°C should access recovery.
The proposed regime excludes kinetically or thermodynamically significant grain-boundary segregation and impurity effects.
Aging changes the B2 phase from a continuous coherent network to a discontinuous semi-coherent or incoherent network.
Ductility reaches a distinct minimum at the aging condition with the peak density of coherent ordered domains.
The ductility minimum is accompanied by a sharp increase in yield strength and a reduction in strain-hardening capacity.
The as-cast or solutionized baseline has moderate ductility because it lacks a percolating ordered network and its fine phase boundaries permit dislocation glide.
The embrittlement regime is bounded by simultaneous B2/FCC coherency and percolating local order, ending when cross-slip or loss of phase-boundary coherency becomes dominant.
Observation of free single-dislocation glide through ordered B2 without superdislocations, or incoherent source/sink phase boundaries in the embrittled state, would falsify the hypothesis.
Observation of segregation-driven grain-boundary cracking without local-order evolution would falsify the proposed non-grain-boundary mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism say B2 coarsening creates a continuous, coherent, percolating network at intermediate aging conditions, whereas the structural mediator describes aging as a transition from a continuous coherent network to a discontinuous semi-coherent or incoherent network. The direction and timing of the morphology change are not reconciled.

High-energy or high-density APBs are said to impede dislocations and cause embrittlement, but APB formation at higher temperature is also said to facilitate bypass and recovery without explaining why the effect reverses.

Mechanical testing is specified at room temperature after aging, yet recovery is attributed to thermal activation of cross-slip at the higher aging temperature. Cross-slip during aging cannot directly accommodate tensile deformation performed later at room temperature unless a persistent microstructural change is identified.

The recovery mechanism alternates among cross-slip, APB formation, loss of coherency, and phase-boundary decohesion. Decohesion is not equivalent to benign loss of coherency and would ordinarily imply interface separation rather than easier dislocation transmission.
